summary:
Samsun is a province on Turkey's Black Sea coast. No province-specific rule, ban or enforcement programme targeting transgender visitors is recorded there; what applies in Samsun is the national framework that governs every other province.

That framework contains no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers, so the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor, that requirement meets street-level identity checks: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One detainee's account records that nothing was fined, but names and details were taken, and that officers were already applying a regime that had not been enacted.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Article 40 of the Civil Code, with the applicant at least 18 years old, unmarried and holding a medical report issued by a state-designated hospital. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation is therefore dealing with a country where recognised gender change is possible but court-gated and medically conditioned.

Criminalisation by statute had not been enacted when Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025, but the leaked 11th Judicial Package then before the government would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, and participation in same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years. Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet analyses the same 66-page draft, leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025, which amends the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws. It is the third set of proposed amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care and for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25, add infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers of gender-affirming care for up to 7 years and patients for up to 3 years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility at scale is recorded in the Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025: 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions — 256 on the record and 43 off it — alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Turkish Minute's coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected.

Policing asymmetry recurs in individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Event attendance carries its own exposure: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
The draft package sits inside a broader authoritarian drift that the Erdoğan government has underwritten by repeatedly framing LGBT people as threats to 'the family' and 'public morals', a framing legal analysts treat as legitimising stigmatisation rather than as isolated moral legislation.

Assembly rights for LGBT events have moved in one direction: Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013 and 2014, the 2015 to 2018 parades were banned by local authorities, and the monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found violations of international human-rights law that have continued since 2015. Attendance at a Pride event is therefore a documented exposure point rather than a routine civic activity.

The military bars homosexuals from service and treats homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness, a classification that extends the medicalised frame applied to gender recognition under Civil Code Article 40.

The pattern of case-level asymmetry in policing is comparable to documented responses elsewhere in the region, but the sources do not present a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction comparison of how trans visitors are treated at checkpoints.

Residents of Samsun answer to the same legal gender recognition process as the rest of the country: an application to a court under Article 40 of the Civil Code, the applicant at least 18 and unmarried, supported by a medical report from a state-designated hospital. Sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988 and homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858.

The 11th Judicial Package, if enacted, would raise that threshold to 25 years of age, add infertility and repeated-evaluation requirements, and expose patients to up to 3 years' imprisonment and providers to up to 7 years for gender-affirming care. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have objected to the draft.

Residents are counted in the same monitoring data: 313 recorded violations in 2025, of which 299 were detention decisions, and six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence, three classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected.

Detention conditions fall on residents as on visitors: facilities are organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, with arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation, restricted healthcare, no staff training on LGBTI+ needs, ineffective complaints mechanisms and frequent transfers. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 prompted demands from rights groups for an independent investigation; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 is unresolved in the sources available for this record.

The sources contain no Samsun-specific reporting on police identity checks, ID enforcement at transit checkpoints, or local treatment of trans visitors; the checkpoints and the August 2025 stops documented here occurred in Istanbul, and are cited as the national pattern a visitor to Samsun would fall under.

No figure is sourced for how often the 3,000-lira ID fine is actually imposed on foreign trans travellers, nor whether any detention of a foreign national on those grounds has occurred in Samsun.

It is not sourced whether provincial courts in Samsun handle Article 40 petitions differently from courts elsewhere, or what processing times a visitor-relevant gender-marker dispute would face.
